Where else can I get a york compressor?
You can get a new or remanufactured compressor from Autozone (tell the clerk you need an AC compressor for one of the above applications)
You can also get one from Kilby Enterprises at www.onboardair.com. Expect to pay $100 without clutches for a york new/remanufactured, and do not pay over 50-60 with clutches from a boneyard. My friend got mine for $23 from a junkyard in daytona beach, and shipped it to me for $10. Total investment = $33

I have my compressor, now what do I need to get it mounted and in place?

Brackets:

You need to mount this thing somehow. Decide weather you want to run it off your alternator, in your serpentine belt rotation, or anywhere else (i have seen driveshaft, but not the best idea, lol).
Depeding on what you drive, you may or may not be in luck. Onboard Air and Air Ride Technologies sell brackets for popular applications. Mine was a 1988 4.3L OBS with a 4 groove serpentine setup. There were no
premanufactured brackets for my application, so i was forced to make my own. Remember when making your own brackets, that this thing needs to be solid! I cannot emphisize that enough. When this thing is pumping, there is some serious vibration.

Clutches:

You need to get the proper clutch set for your compressor. You need to decide how you will mount it, and that determines what clutches you will need.
If you want to run your york in your serpentine belt rotation, you will need a serpentine clutch . I have a V-belt clutch on my york, because i run
a Kilby Combo Pully


I have my york mounted, how do i plumb it?

You need to get some way of converting the rotolock thread flanges to NPT so you can run standard fittings off of it. The easiest way to do this is to order these flanges from onboardair. There are also flanges that screw over the exsisting rotolock thread.


Stainless Braided Line:
You NEED ATLEAST 3ft of stainless braided line coming off of the flanges. The air coming out of a york is very hot, and the stainless line helps dissapate the heat. I got 3 ft of stainless line from www.mcmaster.com. Cost = $36.
You can get the stainless line from ART, but i do not know the link.

Check Valve
The air coming out of a york is pressurized... duh. To prevent that pressure from coming back and blowing your york up, you need a check valve. You can get check valves just about anywhere. Try larry @ innovative or jason @ suicidedoors.


Fittings and other crap
I then run a compression fitting to run my DOT air line off of my check valve. This line then goes into a water trap, which goes into your air tank.
You also need an intake filter, because like anything else with a machined surface inside, you need to filter the air before it gets in.




Misc Crap to know about yorks


They spew alot of oil.
Because you are converting what once was a closed system into a open system, oil needs to escape somewhere. There are a few options, you can do the Oil Mod, or you can get an oil seperating unit from onboardair.com.
Read that Oil Mod link, as it is very informative.

Oil and maintence
Because of the oil escaping, you need the oil your compressor. I use 30W non-detergent oil, and a kilby dipstick to check to make sure it is full. A full compressor takes around 14 ounces of oil, and the kilby dipstick has a mark in it for every ounce of oil in the compressor.

Wiring
You wire your compressor is easy. With anything electrical, there are a few ways of doing it. I prefer mine to be manual, so i can control what RPM's my compressor comes on at, so i just wired a fuse inbetween the clutch wire and a switch that I use to turn the compressor on and off.
You can also use a pressure switch if you prefer, but make sure you use a relay. Do not hack wiring.

post_rewrites.rewritten_content:
Here are some cars that feature York compressors:

- Many pre-1984 Volvos, particularly models with a 210 engine.
- American Motors Ambassador (1963-1968)
- American (1963-1966)
- American Marlin (1965-1967)
- American Rebel (1967-1968)
- Audi 4000 5-cylinder (2.2L) (1980-1984), Audi 4000S Quattro 5-cylinder (2.2L) (1984)
- Audi Coupe 5-cylinder (2.3L) (1987), Audi Coupe 5-cylinder (2.2L) (1981-1987)
- Ford Custom (various years and engine sizes, including 8-cylinder models from 1964 to 1969)
- Ford Fairlane (various years and engine sizes, including 8-cylinder models from 1958 to 1970)
- Ford Falcon (various years and engine sizes, including 8-cylinder models in the late 1960s)
- Ford Galaxie (various years and engine sizes, including 8-cylinder models in the mid-to-late 1960s)
- Ford LTD (various years and engine sizes, including 8-cylinder models from 1967 to 1969)
- Ford Maverick (1970)
- Ford Mustang (1967 to 1970)
- Ford Thunderbird (8-cylinder versions from 1963 to 1968)
- Ford F-Series and E-Series light trucks (various years, including 8-cylinder models in the late 1960s to early 1970s)
- Ford International Scout II (4-cylinder and various 8-cylinder models from 1973 to 1978)
- Lincoln Continental (1963-1965, 1966-1968)
- Mercedes-Benz (various models and years, including some 6-cylinder and 8-cylinder versions)

For a complete list, refer to the original source.

To mount and install your compressor, you'll need brackets to secure it. Decide if you want to run the compressor off your alternator or in your serpentine belt rotation; homemade brackets may be necessary for some vehicles. For my 1988 4.3L OBS with a 4-groove serpentine setup, I had to create custom brackets due to the lack of pre-manufactured ones.

You must select the appropriate clutch based on your mounting location. A serpentine clutch is needed if you plan to use the compressor in this belt rotation; I used a V-belt clutch with my Kilby Combo Pulley.

To plumb the system, convert the rotolock thread flanges to NPT for standard fittings using brackets from Onboard Air or ART. For heat dissipation and to prevent excessive pressure, install at least 3 feet of stainless braided line and a check valve. Fittings should connect your check valve to the DOT air line leading into a water trap and then to your air tank.

An intake filter is essential for filtering air before it enters the system. The York compressor expels significant oil; consider an oil mod or oil separating unit from Onboard Air, as detailed in their documentation.

Regularly check the oil level with 30W non-detergent oil using a Kilby dipstick. A full compressor requires about 14 ounces of oil.

For wiring, I prefer a manual setup, adding a switch between the clutch wire and fuse for control over RPMs. Alternatively, use a pressure switch and relay if preferred. Ensure proper and safe electrical connections.

For more detailed information, refer to these resources:
- [Truck Air](http://www.geocities.com/spencerhut/truck/air.htm)
- [University of Jeep](http://www.universityofjeep.ca/oba_install_paul.html)
- [Slowzuki](http://moose.ca/~slowzuki/slowzuki/t...omp/OilFix.htm)
- [Jedi.com](http://www.jedi.com/obiwan/jeep/york_lube.html)
- [Compressor Service Manual](http://www.ccicompressor.com/SrvcManl.htm)
- [Off-Road.com](http://www.off-road.com/jeep/tech/body/york/)
- [Rock Crawler Tech Report Part 1](http://www.rockcrawler.com/techrepor...art1/york2.htm)

Hope this helps!

When ordering fittings from Onboard Air, be sure to request the O-rings as they are included but must be specifically asked for. Pictures of a TBI with a 210 York installation in the stock location under the AC system hood are available on my SD site. Note that this truck is a non-AC model from the factory.

This thread would make a great sticky. It focuses on modifications for Yorkshire setups, particularly regarding onboard air conversion. My setup includes a custom bracket, a 210 and V-belt clutch, and a tensioner pulley that is a regular idler pulley pushed down in a slot. I also use an Overdrive Kilby combo pulley and Top Rotolock/tube-o fittings for the air system. Additionally, I replaced my 105-amp alternator with a larger case 140-amp unit, which required a new rear bracket (an O.E. part from GM for trucks with a 140-amp O.E. alternator; available for $5 from a GM dealership). Here are some pictures: custom bracket setup, unmounted setup, installed setup.

I thought this thread could be helpful for many people, but it quickly fell to the bottom after just a few seconds, which disappointed me. It seems like older threads with fewer posts receive more attention. I'll move on.

Great post, and it definitely deserves to be sticky! I was curious though: If you're using a mini-York with a 209 or 206 compressor instead of a 210, does the oil fix modification still apply? But only if the compressor originally came from an A/C setup and wasn't built for on-board air (like airride or tool operation), correct?

Great post; it should definitely be sticky. Regarding the oil fix mod for mini York compressors like the 209 and 206, this is only necessary if the compressor originally came from an AC setup and wasn't designed for on-board air (airride or tool operation). Even when purchased for onboard air use, these compressors were typically built with AC in mind. It’s not recommended to perform the oil mod on a new York compressor; instead, break it in first before making any modifications. I recently discovered that my compressor still had high and low pressure lines attached. My father mentioned that cutting the crimped band on these hoses would reveal barbs underneath. Following his advice, I removed the bands, and indeed found barbed ends. Now, I am recrimping one hose with high-temperature tubing and adding an NPT fitting. This approach is more cost-effective than purchasing all necessary adaptors and steel braided lines.
Yes, NAPA and other stores can crimp hoses for you.

You might also consider contacting businesses that specialize in making or repairing hydraulic hoses. Several such establishments are located in Honolulu, and I occasionally observe their trucks traveling on the freeways en route to job sites for equipment repairs.

I had United Auto Supply create a hydro hose from the front to my tank with 1/2 NPT swivel fittings. It is rated for 210-degree temperature and regular flow, with a 250-degree, ten-minute burst rating. I don't believe I will need a leader hose, as York should not exceed 200 degrees.
